title: Kefir
description: Fermented milk drink made from kefir grains
wiki_lead:
Kefir ( kə-FEER; alternative spellings: kephir or kefier) is a fermented milk drink similar to a thin yogurt or ayran that is made from kefir grains, a specific type of mesophilic symbiotic culture. It is prepared by inoculating the milk of cows, goats, or sheep with kefir grains.
Kefir is a common breakfast, lunch or dinner drink consumed in countries of West Asia and Central and Eastern Europe. Kefir is consumed at any time of the day, alongside Central Asian breads like shelpek (Kazakh bread), burek and banitsa/gibanica, and is an ingredient in cold soups.

Kefir ( kə-FEER; alternative spellings: kephir or kefier) is a fermented milk drink similar to a thin yogurt or ayran that is made from kefir grains, a specific type of mesophilic symbiotic culture. It is prepared by inoculating the milk of cows, goats, or sheep with kefir grains.
Kefir is a common breakfast, lunch or dinner drink consumed in countries of West Asia and Central and Eastern Europe. Kefir is consumed at any time of the day, alongside Central Asian breads like shelpek (Kazakh bread), burek and banitsa/gibanica, and is an ingredient in cold soups.


Origin and etymology
Kefir has been found in graves in the Bronze Age Xiaohe Cemetery, dating back 3,600 years.
The word kefir is of North Caucasian origin, where related words are attested in several languages: Mingrelian ქიფური (kipuri), Karachay-Balkar гыпы (gıpı) and Ossetian къӕпы (k'æpy). One theory is that the word comes from Old Turkic köpür '(milk) froth'. It was loaned into Russian where it is attested since 1870s, and from there it was loaned into English, there attested in 1880s. It has become an internationalism, as it is found in many European languages.
Kefir is a very popular drink in the North Caucasus, it is a part of traditional Circassian cuisine to this day. Traditional kefir was made in goatskin bags that were hung near a doorway; the bags would be knocked by anyone passing through to keep the milk and kefir grains well mixed. In Karachay-Balkar, gıpı has a connection with gıpıt (wineskin). It was under the name wineskin that Karachay kefir was distributed in the second half of the 19th century and at the beginning of the 20th century. Kefir spread from the former Soviet Union to the rest of Europe, Canada, Japan, and the United States by the early 21st century.


Fermentation and kefir grain formation

Traditional kefir is fermented at ambient temperatures, generally overnight. Fermentation of the lactose yields a sour, carbonated, slightly alcoholic beverage, with a consistency and taste similar to drinkable yogurt.
The kefir grains initiating the fermentation are initially created by auto-aggregations of Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens and Maudiozyma turicensis or M. humilis, where multiple biofilm producers cause the surfaces to adhere which form a three dimensional microcolony. The biofilm is a matrix of heteropolysaccharides called kefiran, which is composed of equal proportions of glucose and galactose. It resembles small cauliflower grains, with color ranging from white to creamy yellow. A complex and highly variable symbiotic community can be found in these grains, which can include acetic acid bacteria (such as Acetobacter aceti and Acetobacter rasens), yeasts (such as Kluyveromyces lactis, K. marxianus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, M. turicensis) and a number of Lactobacillus species, such as L. parakefiri, L. kefiranofaciens (and subsp. kefirgranum), L. kefiri, L. brevis, etc. While some microbes predominate, Lactobacillus species are always present. grok_lead: Kefir is a fermented dairy beverage produced through the inoculation of milk with kefir grains (also known in Spanish-speaking regions as bÃºlgaros de leche or simply bÃºlgaros, yogur bÃºlgaro, or leche kefirada), which consist of a symbiotic matrix of bacteria and yeasts that ferment the milk into a tangy, effervescent, and slightly alcoholic drink with a creamy consistency. Traditionally associated with the Caucasus Mountains region of Eastern Europe and Southwest Asia, where it has been consumed for centuries, recent archaeological evidence from Bronze Age China suggests similar microbial fermentations date back approximately 3,500 years. The production of kefir involves fermenting milk with kefir grains at around room temperature for about a day, yielding a probiotic -rich beverage. Kefir's diverse microbial community contributes to its unique texture and potential health properties. Kefir is nutritious, providing protein, fats, carbohydrates, calcium, and bioactive compounds like kefiran. It is linked to health benefits such as improved digestion and gut health. Contrary to some popular claims, particularly in certain regional sources, that kefir physically coats or envelops the stomach to form a protective layer, scientific evidence shows no such physical barrier formation or direct increase in gastric mucus secretion attributable to kefir itself. Instead, kefir provides gastroprotective effects through its probiotics, antioxidant activity, and reduction of oxidative stress and inflammation, helping prevent gastric ulcers and damage in animal models. Preclinical studies, including a 2025 study demonstrating that heat-killed Lentilactobacillus kefiri from kefir reduced chronic inflammation in aged mice by lowering IL-6 and TNF-Î± levels, showing anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and other effects; however, human studies specifically on aging remain limited. Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials have shown that kefir consumption significantly reduces fasting blood glucose (mean differences of -8.46 to -10.28 mg/dL) and insulin resistance (e.g., HOMA-IR MD = -1.71), supporting potential benefits for glycemic control and metabolic health, although effects on lipids, anthropometrics, and inflammation are often non-significant or limited. Recent human clinical trials (as of 2025) further support benefits for blood pressure and inflammation reduction. In its native regions, kefir has long been valued as a healthful elixir, and its popularity has grown worldwide due to probiotic recognition.
